I called this right here on Voat a couple of months ago. It's not that Trump has done anything illegal. He's made his money chiefly as a real estate investor and the whole point of real estate investment is that you take your profits out of the future growth of property value through periodic refinance because the proceeds from loans aren't taxable. That's how the business works. It may be asshattery, but it's not 'wrong' or unusual.

Real estate is normally developed on loans (ie. other people's money) and, as long as conditions in the real estate market are normal, every time you build or renovate something the collective value of the property immediately goes up about 20% based on the assumption that you've 'improved' the property. There's no strictly logical or physical reason for that. It's a market convention like the way a 30-40% markup on retail goods is considered reasonable. But it's the whole basis of real estate speculation. And after you build something you refinance a year or two later and take that 20% out from the new loan. The proceeds of loans aren't taxable. It's not 'income' or 'profit' under tax law. So imagine you've spent $10 million of other people's money and and walk away with $2 million tax-free. And every time you do this, the properties you hold add to your credit rating, so you can do it again and again. As long as the real estate market is growing, you can refinance your property every several years, over and over, maybe do a little renovation to keep rents strong, and take more money out, tax free. It's a little weird, but you're actually living on future value.

Real estate investors normally don't try to profit on rent because rental income is taxable. So they operate buildings to break-even on their maintenance. They want rent to exactly cover the loan payments, property taxes, and operating costs of the building and no more. Anything extra is going to get taxed, and that's just a waste of money. If you are doing things 'right' as a real estate investor, you should never pay income tax. So when Trump says something like; " I don't pay taxes because I'm smart" he's not wrong. He's doing his job, even if he's being an asshole about it. It's a little tricky to maintain this balance, and during those, at one time rare, incidences of real estate market downturns you have to know when to bail out and sell the property to a 'greater fool', but if you hire a building management firm, they know how to do this efficiently so it all runs more-or-less on autopilot. There's no magic or skill to any of this. It's so easy even a Trump can do it.

The thing is, if you try to explain this to the public the ethics of it seem dubious--because they are. Technically, commercial real estate loans are secured by the value of the property being developed and as long as that property value is always growing, the rental market is healthy, and you're hiring contractors and property managers all approved by the bank, there's little risk. It's really hard to screw this up--though Trump has, repeatedly, because he gets into more risky kinds of real estate like casinos. But he never actually suffers the consequences since the law gives rich folks so many ways to own things without having actual responsibility for them. This also scales quite easily. There are lots of one-house-at-a-time real estate investors. That's very popular for independent contractors who can put in their own spare labor and materials for free. Everyone could do what Trump does for a living were it not for the fact that, if everyone did, the whole real estate racket would collapse. So banks choose who gets access to this kind of enormous credit--and it's not you. If the basis of their choice isn't merit, what is it? Class. That's a political liability because it's, fundamentally, un-American.

In the past, before they were allowed to dabble in the stock market, banks used to give their rich customers what were called 'self-liquidating loans'. Folks would go into a bank and say; "I'm so and so of the such and such family and I need 100 grand." And the banker would say; "OK, let's give you a loan for 100 grand plus this much more that will be put into a mutual fund securing the loan so that the yield on the fund pays your loan payments automatically." And so the person walks out of the bank with 100 grand in (tax) free money and as long as the mutual fund performs nominally, they never have to think about it. It pays for itself and goes away. But then we let banks play in the market themselves and this practice sort of faded away--except this is pretty-much the same thing as a commercial real estate loan.

So why didn't banks use this gimmick to end all homelessness? Why couldn't a homeless person go into a bank and ask for money and the bank would say; "OK, we'll take out a loan for you to buy into a mutual fund that secures the loan while the yield on that will pay for the loan and leave you with $30 thousand dollars a year extra to live on." Or why don't they say; "We'll give you a loan for a house that is paid for by periodic refinance on the provision that you sell it back to us when you die. Just try not to burn it down in the meantime..." Why can a bank do pretty much that for rich folk but can't do that for people in need? Class. They can't do it for everybody because then the racket would collapse. They have to draw the line somewhere and bankers favor people just like them. (though, in fact, automation is bringing things to a point where we either figure out how to actually do something very much like this for everybody or the entire world economy comes to a halt. This is what Universal Basic Income is all about)

Rich people--the truly rich--don't usually directly participate in politics for the simple reason that it exposes too much about their lives and where their wealth comes from. She knows the game and she knows her place in it! Trump is an egotistical kook who is putting a key source of wealth at risk by subjecting himself, his businesses, and the basis of his wealth to open public scrutiny. But, life-long, he's never suffered the consequences of any of his own incompetence so he doesn't care. That makes him very dangerous to the rest his class. So if they are actually siding with Hillary, it makes perfect sense.

Trump is a bit different than the usual real estate investor and if you understand this you get some idea of his likely motivations. He's part of a small community of high-profile celebrity real estate investors that emerged in the '80s with the pop-culture hype about 'lifestyles of the rich and famous' inspired by the TV show of that same name--which Trump himself was featured in. These folks specialize in high-profile higher-risk kinds of property--super-luxury apartments, hotels, resorts, and casinos--and cultivate a brand around themselves, using their celebrity to enhance the values of their properties. Put Trump's name on a building and it inflates the value of everything. It will increase the rent and occupancy, increase the rate of property value growth, increases the turn-around value over that usual 20%, increase the potential collateral value of his property portfolio. Everything just gets bigger and bigger. Sometimes Trump doesn't even invest in real estate himself. He just lends his name to other real estate projects who give him a cut for it.

The president of the US is the single greatest celebrity in the entire world. That's the top of the heap in this culture. And so, if Trump becomes president, everything he owns expands enormously in value. His creditworthiness shoots into the stratosphere. He could demand tens of billions from a bank at once and no one would bat an eye. He could become a one man economic singularity. A Capitalist god. And maybe there's a certain bizarre hyper-egotistical altruism in this. Maybe he thinks his brand will actually do for America what it does for his properties. Maybe he thinks that's how he'll make America great again, just like he makes buildings great again when he buys, renovates, and puts his name on them. After all, the US's place in the global economy is not quite objective.

Economists sometimes like to use an analogy to painter Salvador Dali to explain this. Dali had this habit of going into fancy restaurants for a meal and, when getting the bill, would write a check to pay for it. Only he would then doodle some bit of art on the back of it and the restaurant owner would save it rather than cash it, thinking it's future value as a piece of Dali's art would be much greater. And so Dali would get away with all these free meals because, thanks to his fame, no one would cash these checks. And this is pretty much how the dollar's money-market value works and, in a more general sense, America's place in the world economy--only the value of our brand has been in decline in recent years thanks to the blind avarice of the finance community and our ham-fisted foreign policy. So it's possible Trump thinks his brand will reinforce the American brand and lead to restored economic strength through restored 'world market confidence' in America as a whole.
